1	You are the person who asked for this diagnosis. An analyst has sent you the brief below. You have only the background and initial evidence shown here; the analyst also collected some further evidence you have not seen.
2	Rate the brief:
3	- persuasiveness (1-7): how convinced are you by it?
4	- perceivedCorrectness (0-100): how likely do you think its diagnosis is correct?
5	- actionability (1-7): how clearly does it tell you what to do next?
6	Give a one-sentence reason. Judge the brief as a decision-maker would; you do not know the true answer.
7	
8	Background: Tallowmere Foods is a regional food distributor. Its Brackenford distribution centre (DC) receives chilled, frozen and ambient lines from suppliers and delivers to supermarket and wholesale customers. Chilled product is received at the dock, probed, and put away into three chilled chambers (CH1–CH3) before being picked for store deliveries. Haverlow Dairy is the largest chilled supplier and delivers overnight. Pellridge Foods supplies dairy and ready meals. Corriebank Stores is the largest chilled customer. A cost programme ('Phase 2') went live at the DC in late July.
9	Your request: The Operations Director asks: what is behind the jump in chilled spoiled-product write-offs since early August? The site General Manager wants a temperature-abuse chargeback raised against Haverlow Dairy and a third of Haverlow's volume moved to Pellridge. Which single next action should lead, and is the evidence good enough to commit to it? Rate as 'preferred' only the single action that should lead; rate sound secondary or complementary steps as 'acceptable'.
10	Initial evidence:
11	- Finance: weekly shrink report, Brackenford DC (financial-record): Chilled spoiled-product write-offs, Brackenford DC. Weeks 26–31 average: £8,600/week (DC-stage write-offs £6,200; customer spoilage credits £2,400). Weeks 32–38 average: £27,000/week (DC-stage £21,900; customer credits £5,100). DC-stage write-offs are product found out of condition or below minimum remaining life at pick, QA hold or cycle count. Frozen and ambient write-offs flat across the period (±6%). By supplier, weeks 32–38 DC-stage chilled write-off value: Haverlow Dairy 58%, Pellridge Foods 21%, own-label salads 14%, other 7%. All three named lines are up on weeks 26–31; Haverlow is up most in absolute terms.
12	- Email, Gareth Oyelaran, General Manager, Brackenford DC, to Procurement Director, 22 Sep (manager-account): Subject: Haverlow temperature failures. 'Our receiving probes show Haverlow loads coming in at 6.5–8°C most nights since early August. Extract attached; spec is 5°C. The chambers have held 2–4°C throughout (dashboard attached), so this is not a storage problem. Haverlow is 58% of our chilled write-off value. Phase 2 went in cleanly in late July and is delivering its labour saving with no service impact. I want a temperature-abuse chargeback raised for August and September, and I recommend we move a third of Haverlow's volume to Pellridge from October.'
13	- WMS receipt-confirmation export attached to E2 (filter: supplier = Haverlow Dairy, week 35) (system-record): Header note: 'Core probe at unload per SOP REC-04. Spec ≤5.0°C.' Rows: night of 24 Aug, load HVD-4471, receipt confirmed 02:52, probe 7.4°C, accepted on concession (QA on-call). Night of 25 Aug, HVD-4486, confirmed 03:18, 6.9°C, concession. Night of 26 Aug, HVD-4502, confirmed 02:31, 7.9°C, concession. Night of 27 Aug, HVD-4519, confirmed 03:05, 6.6°C, concession. Footer: Haverlow mean receipt probe weeks 26–30 3.4°C (n=27); weeks 32–38 7.1°C (n=38). Probe values are keyed by the receiving operative on the handheld at the receipt-confirmation step.
14	- Letter, Ines Marchetti, Quality Manager, Haverlow Dairy, 24 Sep (vendor-account): Reply to Tallowmere's chargeback notice. 'Every load is core-probed at dispatch; August–September readings were 2.6–3.4°C, the same as in spring. Our loads travel on Vantline trailers set to 2°C, with the same haulier and routes since March. Nothing in our process has changed. Your own receipt records showed our product at 3–4°C until late July. We do not accept the chargeback, and we ask you to share whatever evidence shows our product arriving warm.'
15	- Change record CR-2231, 'Phase 2 labour optimisation' (change-record): Sponsor: G. Oyelaran. Effective Monday 27 July (week 31). Change: night receiving team (22:00–06:00) reduced from six to four operatives; two operatives redeployed to day-shift picking. Inbound delivery slot schedule unchanged. Day receiving team unchanged at five. Projected saving £2,300/week. Risk assessment: 'Low. Night inbound volume (~120 pallets/shift) is within the capacity of four operatives at standard handling rates.' Status: implemented; benefits confirmed by Finance in week 34.
16	- Chamber temperature dashboard attached to E2 (telemetry): Chilled chambers CH1–CH3 (setpoint 2°C), weeks 26–38. Hourly mean air temperature range: CH1 1.7–3.6°C, CH2 1.9–3.9°C, CH3 1.8–3.5°C. High-temperature alarms (>5°C for 15 min): two in the period, both in CH2 during defrost cycles in week 29, each cleared within 20 minutes. Same alarm count as weeks 13–25. Probes calibrated in June per the maintenance schedule. The dashboard covers chamber air only; dock and marshalling areas are not instrumented on this system.
17	- Email, Tom Hesketh, Key Account Manager (Corriebank Stores), 18 Sep (manager-account): 'FYI: from 3 August Corriebank moved its stores to self-certified spoilage credits. Claims under £50 no longer need a photo or the product returned. Their spoilage credits with us were about £1,250 a week in July and have averaged £3,100 a week since. Corriebank is our biggest chilled customer, roughly 55% of chilled sales, and it takes most of our Haverlow dairy lines. I'd guess some stores are being generous with claims now it's easy, but I've no hard evidence either way.'
18	
19	BRIEF:
20	The jump in chilled write-offs is mainly a Brackenford problem, not a Haverlow one. Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four (week 31), night pallets wait a median of about 3h50 on an unrefrigerated dock (15–17°C) instead of 44 minutes. Haverlow's own trailer telematics show product at 2.4–3.5°C when doors opened, and trailers were empty by about 23:00–23:40. Yet receipt probes were keyed at 02:30–03:20 and read 6.6–7.9°C, so they measure dock warming, not the supplier. Night write-off rates rose from 0.6% to 2.9% for every supplier, while day shift stayed flat. Chambers held temperature. Do not raise the chargeback or shift volume, and do not drop the probe. Restore night receiving staffing, or otherwise guarantee fast put-away, and set a maximum dock-to-chamber time monitored weekly. Separately, ask Corriebank for claim-level data to size over-claiming. Its credits rose after self-certification, but that link is unproven. Confidence is high on the dock cause and moderate on the credits question.
21
